---
title: "AS.703 Evaluation"
author: "Brian Powers"
format: pdf
bibliography: references.bib
---

- I chose to study the Los Angeles Police department's predictive policing practices. In the 2010s they had two programs: one using PredPol and one called Operation LASER.
- PredPol was a a place-based, proprietary predictive policing algorithm used between roughly 2011 to April 2020. When it was active, it predicted crime at fine spatial grain (\~500ft grid cells), recalculated per shift. It then directed patrol resources to those predicted cells/hotspots.
- PredPol faced criticism during its implementation.
  - @the-markup_2021_how-we-determined found PredPol predictions disproportionately targeted low-income Black and Latino neighborhoods.
  - Place-based predictive tools trained on police-recorded crime/calls-for-service, not independent crime data [@lum-isaac_2016_to-predict-and-serve].
    - Reported crime is partly a product of policing intensity itself. More patroling means more discovery of low-level offenses, which leads to more recorded incidents. This causes the algorithm to flag that area again, creating a feedback loop.
    - Victim reporting itself is not a clean baseline: reporting rates are suppressed in over-policed and immigrant communities due to distrust of police, so no available data source (police records, calls for service, victimization surveys) offers unpolluted ground truth on true crime location at fine geography.
  - Placed-based algorithms raises Fourth Amendment/equal-protection concerns about concentrated stops rather than classic due-process one. In concentrated stops, no individual is notified or given a chance to contest. DICFP's ACCIC/CAPRA units trace back to Operation LASER's person-based "Chronic Offender" infrastructure [@stop-lapd-spying-coalition_2021_automating-banishment], so DICFP inherits person-based due-process exposure alongside PredPol's place-based legacy.
  - Two competing interpretations of PredPol's role, not resolved by available data: algorithm-as-driver (it independently concentrated policing beyond what existing patrol patterns would have produced) versus algorithm-as-encoder (it encoded pre-existing patrol biases, and the underlying deployment logic didn't change when the algorithm was introduced).
- Ultimately, it was discontinued due to budget constraints driven by the COVID-19 crisis.
  - It was replaced by Data-Informed, Community-Focused Policing (DICFP), launched the same month (April 2020), which LAPD stated aimed to build trust, reduce violent crime, and assist victims [@los-angeles-police-department_2020_data-informed-community-focused].
- The program was only partially transparent.
  - Underlying crime incident and arrest data are public via data.lacity.org (LAPD Crime Incidents, LAPD Arrest data).
  - The algorithm's actual predicted outputs (box-level, per-shift predictions) were not systematically public.
    - Markup only obtained fragments via records requests for specific divisions/periods, not a full city-wide panel.
  - No public data links predicted boxes to actual officer dispatch/patrol behavior.
    - It was impossible to verify whether officers actually complied with or acted on the algorithm's predictions (a mechanism/compliance question).
  - PredPol's lack of transparency could at least partially be attributed to its status as a private vendor. It had no requirement to disclose proprietary model outputs. There was also no systematic public disclosure requirement for algorithmic policing tools' internal predictions or compliance data.
- Overall, this was a poor implementation of predictive policing.
  - The evidence on whether it even achieved its core crime-reduction goal is genuinely contested, not settled.
    - [@mohler-etal_2015_randomized-controlled-field] is the strongest positive evidence: a real randomized controlled trial, including a direct arm within three LAPD divisions (Foothill, North Hollywood, Southwest), found PredPol's ETAS algorithm modestly outperformed analyst-driven hotspot maps (a 7.4% reduction in crime volume as a function of patrol time).
    - That trial has two real limitations. Some authors held a financial stake in PredPol Inc. (a conflict of interest), and the paper does not disclose a random or representativeness-based method for selecting those three divisions. The LAPD has roughly 21. The trial dates track PredPol's actual sequential rollout (Foothill was its original 2011 pilot site), suggesting a convenience sample rather than one chosen to generalize to the department as a whole.
    - Another study directly contradicts it. The RAND Corporation conducted an evaluation and a 2012 Shreveport, LA randomized trial. Both found no statistically significant crime reduction from predictive policing. Early pilot numbers (Atlanta ~8-9% decline, Santa Cruz ~20% burglary decline, Kent ~4% reduction) are vendor/department-reported figures from early adoption, not independently verified at RCT standards.
    - The single best-designed study found a modest positive effect with real caveats, and comparably rigorous independent trials found none.
  - Predictive policing could modestly reduce crime, but the cost might not be worth it. A tool can increase the arrest-to-reported-crime ratio by assigning officers in the area it targets. More patrol produces more arrests. This can happen even as citywide crime falls in aggregate. Reducing crime overall and increasing local overpolicing are not contradictory findings; they can be the same mechanism described from two different angles.
  - It is impossible to cleanly attribute any change (or lack of change) after discontinuation to the algorithm specifically. Removal is further confounded by the simultaneous George Floyd protests and national policing reckoning, on top of the COVID-19 budget crisis already noted above.
  - What should they have done instead?
    - If crimes are significantly underreported, then any tool that gets its data from reported crimes will be systematically biased. Fixing that bias requires crime data independent of policing intensity. This kind of data is precise and granual, and it is not publicly collected.
    - Instead, data should be collected by a team of independent researchers or community organizations to survey where crime is over- or under-reported. This would allow enforcement intensity to be checked against something other than the police's own contaminated data.
